note: Changing only the numbers in a maths question degraded every model tested, and adding one irrelevant clause cut performance by up to 65 percent. Widely cited as evidence that benchmark scores overstate reasoning.
title: GSM-Symbolic: Understanding the Limitations of Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models

reading.body:
Changing only the numbers in a grade-school math question degraded every model tested, and adding one irrelevant clause cut performance by as much as 65 percent.

This is a direct challenge to how reasoning claims get made. If a model's accuracy depends on the exact numbers or phrasing of a question rather than the underlying logic, then benchmark scores are measuring something closer to pattern matching against familiar problem shapes than genuine mathematical reasoning. The size of the drop, up to 65 percent from one irrelevant clause, is what makes this widely cited as evidence that reported reasoning scores overstate real capability.

The data does not identify which architectures are more or less affected, or whether the effect shrinks with model scale, only that it was present across the models tested.

explain_beginner: Researchers tested whether popular AI systems can actually do math reasoning or if they're just pattern-matching what they've seen before. They created new math problems by changing numbers and adding extra information to existing questions. They found that all tested AI models performed worse when numbers changed, even though the math stayed the same. Adding one unnecessary sentence dropped accuracy by up to 65 percent. This suggests the models aren't truly reasoning mathematically but instead copying shortcuts learned during training.
explain_business: Organizations relying on LLMs for quantitative work should recognize that benchmark scores substantially overstate actual reasoning reliability. Models demonstrate fragility when encountering slightly unfamiliar problem variations or irrelevant information, which reflects real-world conditions. This has implications for deploying these systems in financial analysis, data interpretation, or problem-solving tasks where genuine mathematical reasoning is critical. Decision-makers should implement additional validation and human oversight rather than trusting published performance metrics as indicators of robust reasoning ability.
explain_practitioner: We developed GSM-Symbolic, a benchmark generating diverse problem instantiations from symbolic templates to evaluate mathematical reasoning more rigorously than existing datasets like GSM8K. Testing state-of-the-art open and closed models revealed significant performance variance across different numerical values in identical problem structures. Models exhibited substantial degradation when problem complexity increased or irrelevant clauses were introduced, suggesting they lack genuine logical reasoning and instead rely on memorized patterns. These findings indicate current benchmarks significantly overestimate actual reasoning capabilities.
